cards.title: Rust 1.97.1 fixes LLVM miscompilation in release builds — rebuild anything shipped with 1.97.0
cards.summary: An LLVM optimization pass introduced in 1.97.0 silently miscompiles certain release-mode patterns; 1.97.1 reverts it. Any binary you shipped from a 1.97.0 toolchain should be rebuilt and re-released.

cards.title: Langflow default installs have confirmed unauthenticated RCE actively exploited in the wild
cards.summary: CVE-2026-9198 allows a remote attacker to execute arbitrary code on a default Langflow deployment with no credentials; CISA has added it to KEV with a federal remediation deadline. Patch immediately or network-isolate any Langflow instance — default configurations are the attack surface.

cards.title: Claude Sonnet 5 price increase cancelled — $2/$10 per MTok is now the permanent rate
cards.summary: Anthropic has confirmed the previously announced September 1 hike to $3/$15 per MTok will not occur; $2/$10 is locked in. Revert any budget headroom or cost-model adjustments you made in anticipation of the increase.

cards.title: GPT-5.6 Fast mode now accepts prompts over 272K tokens with up to 2.5× throughput
cards.summary: Setting `service_tier: "fast"` on requests longer than 272K tokens now works, unlocking fast-mode pricing and throughput for large-document RAG and batch summarisation pipelines that were previously forced into Standard. The throughput gain versus Standard is up to 2.5× with the same latency trade-off that applies to shorter fast-mode requests.

cards.title: Meta ships Muse Code public beta — terminal coding agent with parallel sub-agents and worktree isolation
cards.summary: Muse Code runs parallel sub-agents, confines each to an isolated worktree, and writes all operations to a crash-safe event log designed for large-repo tasks. Public beta is open with API access; sub-agent orchestration APIs and the event-log schema are documented for tooling integration.

cards.title: OpenAI sets December 11 hard removal date for o3 and older GPT-5 API snapshot strings
cards.summary: Named o3 and older GPT-5 snapshot model identifiers will return errors after December 11, 2026; the o3 model selector in ChatGPT disappears August 26. Audit evals, CI prompts, and any production integration pinned to specific snapshot strings and migrate to current aliases before the deadline.

cards.title: CSS `transform` on an Ancestor Silently Breaks `position: fixed`
cards.summary: Adding a CSS transform to any ancestor element creates a new containing block, causing `position: fixed` children to position relative to that ancestor instead of the viewport — a spec-compliant behavior that routinely breaks modals and tooltips when animations are added later.
cards.body: The CSS spec defines that `transform`, `filter`, `perspective`, `backdrop-filter`, or `will-change` with any of those values causes an element to establish a containing block for all descendants — including fixed-positioned ones. This means a `position: fixed` tooltip inside an animated card wrapper is no longer anchored to the viewport at all. The bug typically surfaces when a designer adds a hover animation (`transform: scale(1.02)`) to a card that happens to contain a dropdown or tooltip, and those elements suddenly jump to wrong positions. The only reliable fix is to move fixed-positioned overlays outside the transformed subtree in the DOM, often via a portal.

cards.title: TypeScript's Excess Property Check Is Bypassed by Intermediate Variables
cards.summary: TypeScript only runs excess property checking when an object literal is assigned directly to a typed target; assigning via an intermediate variable silently drops the check, meaning typo'd or unknown keys are accepted without error.
cards.body: Excess property checking is a special syntactic rule that fires only on fresh object literals at the point of assignment — it is not part of structural type compatibility. When you store an object literal in an intermediate `const` first, TypeScript widens it to its inferred type and then checks structural compatibility only, which does not flag extra properties. This is why a misspelled option key (e.g., `retries` on a type that expects `retry`) can silently pass through and be ignored at runtime with zero compiler feedback. The practical implication: wrapper functions that accept `options: SomeConfig` will not catch extra keys if callers build their options object separately before passing it.

cards.title: Node.js `cluster` Workers Have Independent Heaps — In-Process State Never Syncs
cards.summary: The `cluster` module forks OS processes, not threads, so every worker starts with a copy of the heap and then diverges. Any in-memory structure — rate-limit counters, feature flags, session maps — becomes silently per-worker, multiplying your effective limits by the worker count.
cards.body: Node's `cluster.fork()` calls `fork(2)` under the hood, giving each worker a private address space. A `Map` that tracks request counts will count independently in each of your four workers, so a rate limit of 100 will actually allow 400 requests before any single worker rejects. This is the same reason sticky sessions exist: load balancers that don't pin a client may route the same user to a worker with no session state. Any coordination — rate limiting, distributed locks, pub/sub fan-out — needs an external store like Redis.

cards.title: `multiprocessing` `fork` Copies Open DB Connections into Child Processes
cards.summary: On Linux, Python's default `fork` start method clones the parent including any open sockets and database connection pools. Both parent and child then race to use the same underlying TCP stream, causing protocol corruption or ghost queries with no exception raised.
cards.body: When `multiprocessing.Pool` forks, the child process inherits file descriptors byte-for-byte, including SQLAlchemy engine pools, psycopg2 connections, and Redis sockets. The parent and child then both write to the same kernel socket buffer, interleaving protocol frames. The database sees malformed packets and may silently return wrong results, drop the connection, or deadlock. The safe fix is `multiprocessing.set_start_method('spawn')` (slower, clean slate) or disposing the engine in a pool initializer before any child work begins.
cards.code:
import multiprocessing
from sqlalchemy import create_engine, text

engine = create_engine("postgresql+psycopg2://...")  # opened at import time

def worker(item_id):
    # engine's pool was copied from parent — parent and child share sockets
    with engine.connect() as conn:  # silently reuses corrupted fd
        return conn.execute(text("SELECT * FROM items WHERE id=:id"), {"id": item_id}).fetchone()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    multiprocessing.set_start_method("spawn")  # clean process, no inherited fds
    with multiprocessing.Pool(4) as pool:
        results = pool.map(worker, item_ids)

cards.title: `ThreadLocal` Values Persist Across Tasks in a Thread Pool
cards.summary: Thread pools reuse threads, so a `ThreadLocal` set during one task is still visible to the next task that runs on the same thread — potentially from a different user or tenant. The value is never cleared automatically; you must call `remove()` in a `finally` block.
cards.body: `ThreadLocal` storage lives on the `Thread` object itself and has no concept of task boundaries. When a request sets a security context, database tenant ID, or trace ID into a `ThreadLocal` and the request handler returns without calling `remove()`, the next `Runnable` dequeued by that thread picks up a stale value. This is how tenant data bleeds across requests in shared-pool architectures. Frameworks like Spring's `RequestContextHolder` handle cleanup for you inside the servlet lifecycle, but code outside that lifecycle — async tasks, custom `ExecutorService` submissions — does not get the same treatment.

cards.title: `time.After` Inside a Loop Leaks a New Timer on Every Iteration
cards.summary: `time.After` allocates a `time.Timer` internally each time it is called and that timer is not garbage-collected until it fires. In a `select` loop where another case regularly wins, you accumulate thousands of live timers that hold memory until their full duration elapses.
cards.body: The Go runtime parks each `time.After` channel in a min-heap until the deadline; it has no way to know you've moved on to the next loop iteration. In a high-throughput message loop with a five-second idle timeout, every message arrival that triggers the `msg` case leaves a five-second timer still ticking. Under load you can hold millions of goroutine-seconds of unreleased timers. The fix is to allocate one `time.NewTimer` before the loop and call `Reset` after each use, checking the channel drain requirement the Go docs spell out.

cards.title: Snapshot Isolation Allows Write Skew Even When Every Individual Read Looks Consistent
cards.summary: Under snapshot isolation (PostgreSQL's default), two concurrent transactions each see a consistent snapshot at their start time, so both can read the same rows, independently conclude an invariant holds, and each write different rows — with neither seeing the other's write. The invariant breaks at commit time.
cards.body: This anomaly is called write skew and it's distinct from a dirty read or non-repeatable read. The classic example: two transactions both check that at least one doctor is on call, each sees two doctors, and each removes one — leaving zero. Neither transaction did anything 'wrong' from its own snapshot's perspective. Preventing it requires `ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE`, which adds predicate locking and rolls back one of the conflicting transactions with a serialization error you must retry. `REPEATABLE READ` in Postgres is snapshot isolation and does not prevent write skew.
cards.code:
-- T1 and T2 run concurrently; both see alice=oncall, bob=oncall (count = 2)

-- T1
BEGIN; -- snapshot: alice ON, bob ON
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM doctors WHERE oncall; -- 2, safe to remove one
UPDATE doctors SET oncall = false WHERE name = 'alice';
COMMIT; -- succeeds

-- T2 (concurrent)
BEGIN; -- same snapshot: alice ON, bob ON
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM doctors WHERE oncall; -- still 2 in its snapshot
UPDATE doctors SET oncall = false WHERE name = 'bob';
COMMIT; -- also succeeds → 0 doctors on call

-- Fix:
BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;
-- one transaction will abort with SQLSTATE 40001; application must retry

cards.title: Publishing to a Message Broker After `COMMIT` Creates an Invisible Split-Brain Window
cards.summary: Calling `kafka.send()` or `rabbitmq.publish()` immediately after a successful database commit looks safe but creates a gap: a crash, OOM kill, or network failure between the two writes leaves the DB updated with no event emitted and consumers permanently behind.
cards.body: The two operations — database commit and broker publish — cannot be wrapped in a single distributed transaction without a two-phase commit coordinator, which almost no production stack uses. The transactional outbox pattern sidesteps this by inserting the event as a row in an `outbox` table inside the same local transaction as the business write. A separate relay process (Debezium reading the WAL, or a polling job) reads committed outbox rows and publishes them, delivering at-least-once guarantees. Consumers deduplicate on an `event_id`. The relay is the only component that needs to be reliable; the application itself stays simple.

cards.title: A client retries a payment request after a network timeout, but the first request actually succeeded. How do you prevent the customer from being charged twice?
cards.summary: Tests whether the candidate treats idempotency as a first-class distributed-systems primitive — not just deduplication, but the storage, scoping, expiry, and concurrency tradeoffs of idempotency keys.
cards.body: Assign every mutation a client-generated idempotency key (typically a UUID) and store it atomically alongside the result in the same database transaction that processes the payment. Before executing, look up the key: if it exists, return the stored response without re-executing. Keys must be scoped narrowly (e.g., per-account) for fast lookups and given a TTL so the key store doesn't grow unbounded. The critical detail is that the key write and the side-effecting write must share a transaction boundary — if they're in separate stores, a crash between them re-opens the double-charge window. For downstream exactly-once delivery, pair this with the transactional outbox pattern: write the event to an outbox table in the same commit, then relay it asynchronously via a change-data-capture process. This design makes retries safe at every layer — client, load balancer, and internal service calls.
followUps: What happens if two retries carrying the same idempotency key arrive concurrently? How do you serialize them without a global lock?
How would you maintain idempotency guarantees across a saga that spans three independently-owned services?
If you use a TTL to expire idempotency keys, what specific failure mode does that reintroduce, and how do you mitigate it?

cards.title: Explain why adding threads to a CPU-bound Python workload can reduce throughput below single-threaded performance, and walk me through how you'd saturate all cores.
cards.summary: Tests whether the candidate understands the GIL's actual contention mechanics — the convoy effect, the switch interval, and the real-world alternatives — rather than just knowing the GIL exists.
cards.body: CPython's Global Interpreter Lock permits only one thread to execute bytecode at a time. For CPU-bound work, multiple threads compete for the GIL every 5 ms (the default switch interval), and the overhead of releasing, signaling, and re-acquiring the lock creates a convoy effect that makes multi-threaded code measurably slower than a single thread. I/O-bound threads dodge this because they release the GIL before entering a blocking syscall. For true CPU parallelism you have three main options: multiprocessing (separate interpreters with separate GILs, at the cost of IPC serialization), C extensions that release the GIL explicitly (NumPy, Cython with nogil blocks), or a ProcessPoolExecutor that gives you a clean futures-based API over process-level parallelism. Python 3.13 shipped an experimental free-threaded build (PEP 703) that removes the GIL entirely, but every C extension must be audited for thread safety, so production adoption is still narrow.
followUps: Why does the GIL not affect I/O-bound threads — what specific mechanism releases it during a socket read or file write?
What are the concrete tradeoffs between multiprocessing with shared memory, a ProcessPoolExecutor, and Cython nogil blocks for a NumPy-heavy pipeline?

cards.title: Explain what a happens-before relationship means in the Java Memory Model and why declaring a field volatile doesn't make check-then-act operations thread-safe.
cards.summary: Tests whether the candidate distinguishes visibility guarantees from atomicity — the exact confusion that produces the majority of Java concurrency bugs in production.
cards.body: A happens-before relationship is a partial ordering guarantee: if action A happens-before action B, then A's memory effects are visible to B. Writing to a volatile field happens-before every subsequent read of that same field, which prevents both stale reads and compiler/CPU reordering across the volatile access. However, volatile provides visibility and ordering only — not atomicity of compound operations. A check-then-act sequence like `if (!flag) { flag = true; doWork(); }` is still a data race: two threads can both observe `false` before either completes the write. To make the compound operation indivisible you need a CAS-based atomic (AtomicBoolean.compareAndSet), a synchronized block, or a Lock. The broader principle is that the JMM defines when writes become visible, not when sequences of reads and writes are mutually exclusive — confusing these two properties is the root cause of most lock-free bugs.
followUps: How does the happens-before chain extend through a ReentrantLock's lock and unlock versus a volatile read and write — are they equivalent in ordering strength?
Describe a realistic scenario where a non-volatile long field is torn on a 32-bit JVM, even though individual word-sized writes are atomic.
When would you prefer a plain volatile boolean over AtomicBoolean, and what do you lose by choosing it?

cards.title: Python Short-Circuit Return Values
cards.summary: Python's `or` and `and` operators return the operand that determined the result, not a boolean.
cards.code:
a = 0 or "" or [] or "hello" or 42
b = 1 and "world" and [] and "foo"
print(a, b)
cards.explanation: Python's `or` returns the first truthy operand (or the last if all are falsy), while `and` returns the first falsy operand (or the last if all are truthy). For `a`, the chain skips 0, "", and [] (all falsy) and returns "hello" — the first truthy value — without ever reaching 42. For `b`, 1 and "world" are truthy, but [] is falsy, so `and` short-circuits and returns [].

cards.title: Array.sort Default Comparison
cards.summary: JavaScript's Array.sort without a comparator converts elements to strings and sorts lexicographically, not numerically.
cards.explanation: When no comparator is supplied, Array.prototype.sort converts each element to a string and compares by UTF-16 code unit order. The string representations are "10", "100", "70", "8", and "9". Lexicographically, "10" < "100" < "70" < "8" < "9" because comparison proceeds character by character, and the code point for '1' is less than '7', which is less than '8'.

cards.title: Go iota with Blank Identifier
cards.summary: Using `_` in a Go const block with iota consumes the counter value without creating a named constant.
cards.explanation: In a Go const block, iota increments by 1 for each constant specification regardless of whether the name is used or discarded. The expression `iota * 2` is implicitly repeated for every subsequent line. A = 0×2 = 0, B = 1×2 = 2, C = 2×2 = 4, the blank identifier _ consumes iota = 3 (value 6, discarded), and D gets iota = 4 so D = 4×2 = 8.

cards.title: Java Switch Fall-Through
cards.summary: Without `break` statements, Java's switch falls through every subsequent case and default after the first match.
cards.explanation: Java's switch statement falls through all subsequent cases once a match is found unless an explicit `break` is encountered. After matching case 1, execution continues unconditionally through case 2, case 3, and default. The accumulation is y = 0 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10. The option 6 corresponds to the wrong belief that `default` is skipped during fall-through; the option 1 corresponds to assuming each case has an implicit break.

cards.title: MCP 2026-07-28 spec removes session state — stateless HTTP is now the standard
cards.summary: Transport-level sessions are gone; servers must be fully stateless and work behind standard HTTP load balancers. The release also adds Multi Round-Trip Requests, header-based routing, cacheable list results, and a formal extensions framework — the largest revision since launch.

cards.title: Go 1.27 ships generic methods, post-quantum crypto, new JSON engine, and UUID stdlib package
cards.summary: Generic methods are now first-class — no more wrapping them as package-level functions. The rewritten `encoding/json` engine and size-specialised malloc (up to 30% cheaper for allocations under 80 bytes) are transparent performance wins requiring no code changes.

cards.title: position: sticky Breaks Silently When an Ancestor Has overflow: hidden
cards.summary: Any ancestor with overflow: hidden, auto, or scroll becomes a scroll container, constraining sticky positioning to that box — which is almost never what you want. Swapping to overflow: clip preserves visual clipping without creating a scroll container.
cards.body: Sticky positioning works by anchoring an element relative to its nearest scrollable ancestor. When a wrapper anywhere up the DOM tree has overflow: hidden, the browser silently promotes that element to the scroll container, so position: sticky is scoped to a box that may never scroll. The element doesn't warn you — it just behaves like position: relative. The fix is overflow: clip, which was designed exactly for this: it clips painted overflow without establishing a new scroll container, so sticky elements can find the real viewport scroller.

cards.title: Object.keys() Returns string[], Not (keyof T)[] — and That's Correct
cards.summary: TypeScript intentionally widens Object.keys() to string[] because structural typing lets objects carry undeclared properties at runtime, making a narrower return type unsound. A typed wrapper trades that soundness warning for ergonomics — know where you're accepting the risk.
cards.body: TypeScript's type system is structural, not nominal: a value typed as { host: string; port: number } may at runtime have additional keys. Returning (keyof T)[] from Object.keys would imply you know every key, which TypeScript cannot guarantee. Casting through a typedKeys helper localises the unsoundness to one place rather than scattering as (keyof T) casts across the codebase. This pattern is safe for objects you construct and own; avoid it for function parameters where callers may pass supertypes.

cards.title: `.pipe()` Silently Abandons Streams on Error
cards.summary: When a stage in a `.pipe()` chain emits an error, Node stops moving data but leaves every other stream open — file handles, sockets, and transform buffers all remain uncollected. `stream.pipeline` wires shared error listeners across every stage and calls `.destroy()` on all of them on the first failure.
cards.body: `.pipe()` listens only for the destination's `end` event and has no built-in error forwarding between stages. An error on a Transform propagates nowhere: the source readable stalls (not closed) and the destination writable stays open, leaking the underlying resource. `stream.pipeline` solves both issues by attaching error listeners to every stream in the chain and destroying all of them on any error. Use `require('stream/promises').pipeline` (Node 15+) to get a promise-returning version that also handles async generators cleanly.

cards.title: `@lru_cache` on Instance Methods Leaks Every Instance
cards.summary: `lru_cache` treats `self` as part of the cache key and holds a strong reference to it, so every object that ever calls the decorated method is pinned in memory for the cache's lifetime — the instance's `__del__` never fires and the GC cannot reclaim it.
cards.body: The decorator stores `(self, *args)` tuples in an internal dict, and dicts hold strong references. Because the cache lives on the class (not the instance), it remains reachable as long as the class itself is loaded — which in practice means forever. For per-instance memoization, `functools.cached_property` stores results directly in the instance's `__dict__`, so they are collected with the instance. For shared memoization, lift the computation to a module-level function that takes only primitive values and cache that instead.

cards.title: `synchronized` Pins Virtual Threads and Kills Loom's Scalability
cards.summary: When a virtual thread enters a `synchronized` block or method, the JVM pins it to its carrier (platform) thread — it cannot unmount even while blocking on I/O. Any blocking call inside a monitor holds a real OS thread, collapsing the scalability benefit of Project Loom.
cards.body: Virtual threads gain their efficiency by unmounting from carrier threads during blocking operations so the carrier can run other virtual threads. `synchronized` uses JVM object monitors, which are bound to carrier-thread identity; the runtime cannot unmount a virtual thread that owns one. Old JDBC drivers, legacy crypto libraries, and any code with blocking I/O inside `synchronized` all trigger pinning. Replace monitors with `ReentrantLock`, which parks cooperatively and allows unmounting. On JDK 21+ you can detect pinning with `-Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=full` or by watching the `jdk.VirtualThreadPinned` JFR event.

cards.title: `http.DefaultClient` Has No Timeout — Goroutines Block Forever
cards.summary: `http.DefaultClient` sets `Timeout` to zero, disabling all deadlines. A server that accepts the TCP connection but never sends a response holds your goroutine open indefinitely, and in a service under load this silently exhausts the goroutine pool or file-descriptor limit.
cards.body: `http.Client.Timeout` covers the entire round-trip: dial, TLS handshake, request write, redirect follows, and reading the full response body. Zero means no limit at any stage. The default client is a shared package-level variable used by `http.Get`, `http.Post`, and friends — one stalled upstream can starve unrelated calls that share the same transport's connection pool. Always construct a named `http.Client` with `Timeout` set. If you need finer control, configure `Transport.DialContext`, `ResponseHeaderTimeout`, and `IdleConnTimeout` separately.

cards.title: Write-Behind Caching Silently Loses Acknowledged Writes on Failure
cards.summary: Write-behind (write-back) caches acknowledge the client write immediately and flush to the database asynchronously — if the cache node crashes before the flush, those writes vanish with no error ever returned to the caller and no record in the DB.
cards.body: The throughput appeal of write-behind is real: batching and coalescing writes before hitting durable storage reduces DB pressure dramatically. The hidden cost is that the cache becomes the system of record for all unflushed mutations, so its durability guarantees now matter as much as the database's. Redis with `appendfsync everysec` (the default AOF mode) can lose up to one second of writes on a crash — silently, because the client already received a success response. Mitigations include `appendfsync always` (serializes all writes through the OS, largely negating the throughput win), using a durable queue like Kafka as the write buffer instead of Redis alone, or reserving write-behind only for genuinely loss-tolerant data such as view counters.
cards.code:
# redis.conf defaults — a crash can drop up to 1 second of acknowledged writes
appendonly yes
appendfsync everysec

# Zero data-loss option — fsync on every write, but kills throughput
# appendfsync always

# Durable alternative: write to Kafka first, consume into DB async
# Cache reflects the committed log, not unsynced memory

cards.title: Modulo Sharding Remaps Nearly Every Key When You Rescale
cards.summary: With `hash(key) % N` sharding, adding one node changes N and therefore reassigns roughly `(N-1)/N` of all keys to different shards — invalidating your entire cache or forcing a full data migration. Consistent hashing limits remapping to approximately 1/N of keys.
cards.body: In a 10-node modulo cluster, `hash(k) % 10` and `hash(k) % 11` agree only when both results happen to be equal, which is about 9% of keys — so a scale-out event silently invalidates ~91% of your cache and thunders those misses straight to the database. Consistent hashing places nodes and keys on a hash ring; adding a node only steals keys from the arc between it and its predecessor. Without virtual nodes, though, physical placement on the ring is uneven and one node may own a disproportionate arc. Assign each physical node V virtual positions (100–150 is common) to smooth the distribution — this is the basis of memcached's ketama, Cassandra's token ranges, and most modern distributed KV stores.

cards.title: You need to enforce a global rate limit of 10,000 req/s across 20 stateless API gateway instances. Walk me through your design and its failure modes.
cards.summary: Tests whether the candidate understands distributed counting, the consistency-latency tradeoff in shared state, and graceful degradation when the coordination layer fails.
cards.body: The standard approach uses a centralized counter in Redis with a sliding-window algorithm—either a sorted set of timestamps or a fixed-window counter with interpolation between the current and previous window. Each gateway atomically increments via a Lua script and checks the result against the threshold. The critical failure mode is Redis going down: you need a fallback, typically a local token bucket per instance pre-loaded with its share of the global budget (500 req/s each). This sacrifices accuracy but prevents both open-flooding and hard-blocking all traffic. A subtler issue is burst traffic at window boundaries; the sliding-window-counter algorithm handles this by weighting the previous window's count, smoothing the edge. You must also address split-brain: if some gateways lose connectivity to Redis while others don't, enforcement becomes inconsistent. The design choice is whether to fail-open (risk over-admission) or fail-closed (risk dropping legitimate traffic), and that decision should be configurable per route.
followUps: How would you handle a sudden failure where 15 of 20 instances go down and the surviving 5 inherit all traffic—does your rate limit still hold?
What's the memory and accuracy tradeoff between a sliding-window-log and a fixed-window-counter approach at high throughput?
How would you extend this to per-tenant limits with 100,000 tenants without exploding your Redis keyspace?

cards.title: Explain how Go's runtime scheduler multiplexes goroutines onto OS threads and what happens when a goroutine makes a blocking system call.
cards.summary: Tests understanding of the GMP scheduling model, the hand-off mechanism for blocking syscalls, and how asynchronous preemption prevents compute-bound goroutines from monopolizing a thread.
cards.body: Go uses an M:N scheduler built around three entities: G (goroutine), M (OS thread), and P (logical processor, capped at GOMAXPROCS). Each P owns a local run queue of runnable Gs. When a goroutine enters a blocking syscall, the runtime performs a hand-off: it detaches the P from the blocked M and assigns it to an idle or newly spawned M so other goroutines keep running. When the syscall returns, the M tries to reacquire a P; if none are free, its G goes to the global run queue and the M parks. For network I/O, the runtime avoids this entirely—the netpoller uses epoll/kqueue to multiplex socket readiness, so network-blocked goroutines never consume an OS thread. Since Go 1.14, the scheduler emits SIGURG-based asynchronous preemption signals, allowing it to pause goroutines stuck in tight compute loops that lack cooperative preemption points. Work stealing across P run queues and periodic checks of the global queue ensure load balance without a centralized lock.
followUps: What class of bugs did non-preemptive scheduling cause before Go 1.14, and how does signal-based preemption solve them?
How does the netpoller integrate with the scheduler so that thousands of concurrent network connections don't each pin an OS thread?

cards.title: Explain how the browser promotes an element to its own compositing layer, what will-change: transform actually does at the rendering pipeline level, and why over-promoting hurts performance.
cards.summary: Tests whether the candidate understands the paint-to-composite pipeline separation and can reason about GPU memory tradeoffs rather than blindly applying optimization hacks.
cards.body: After layout and paint, the compositor decides which subtrees to rasterize into separate GPU-backed textures called layers. Properties like transform, opacity, and filter can be animated entirely on the compositor thread—but only if the element already lives on its own layer. Declaring will-change: transform tells the browser to eagerly promote the element, allocating a dedicated texture and rasterizing it independently. Subsequent transform animations then only require the compositor to reposition the texture, never touching the main thread or triggering repaint. The cost is concrete: every layer consumes GPU memory proportional to its pixel dimensions times device pixel ratio, and the compositor must composite all layers each frame. Over-promoting dozens of elements can exhaust VRAM, trigger fallback to software rasterization, or inflate composite time beyond the frame budget. The correct pattern is to apply will-change shortly before an animation begins and remove it on transitionend or animationend, so layers exist only while they deliver value.
followUps: How would you diagnose excessive layer promotion in DevTools, and which metrics tell you you've crossed the line?
Give an example of implicit layer promotion—where the browser creates a layer you didn't ask for—and explain why it happens.
Why can animating left or top never be compositor-only, even if the element is on its own layer?

cards.title: Closure Over `var` in a Loop
cards.summary: All three closures share the same function-scoped `var i`, which is 3 after the loop ends.
cards.explanation: Because `var` is function-scoped, there is a single `i` binding shared by all three closures. The loop exits when `i` reaches 3, so every closure returns 3. Using `let` instead would create a new binding per iteration, yielding 0, 1, 2.

cards.title: List Repetition and Shared References
cards.summary: The `*` operator on a list of lists copies references, not the inner objects, so mutating one element affects all of them.
cards.explanation: The expression `[[0]] * 3` creates a list containing three references to the same inner list object. Assigning `a[0][0] = 1` mutates that single inner list, and because all three slots point to it, the change is visible in every position. Use a list comprehension like `[[0] for _ in range(3)]` to get independent copies.

cards.title: Slice Append and Shared Backing Array
cards.summary: Appending to a sub-slice that still has capacity overwrites the original slice's backing array instead of allocating a new one.
cards.explanation: The slice literal `s` has len 3 and cap 3. The sub-slice `a = s[:2]` has len 2 but still cap 3, sharing the same backing array. Because there is remaining capacity, `append(a, 4)` writes 4 into the third position of that array, overwriting `s[2]`. A new backing array would only be allocated if `append` exceeded the capacity.

cards.title: Integer Autoboxing Cache Boundary
cards.summary: Java caches `Integer` objects for values −128 to 127; `==` on autoboxed values outside that range compares distinct object references.
cards.explanation: The JLS requires `Integer.valueOf` to cache values from −128 to 127. Autoboxing 127 returns the same cached object for both `a` and `b`, so `==` is true. Autoboxing 128 creates two separate `Integer` objects, so `==` compares references and returns false. Use `.equals()` for reliable value comparison across the full range.

cards.title: npm worm injects self-propagating backdoor into hundreds of packages including keyv
cards.summary: A supply-chain worm has compromised packages with hundreds of millions of weekly downloads by autonomously spreading to dependents—audit your lockfile for affected versions and rotate any secrets that may have been exfiltrated. This is not a theoretical risk; the payload is live in the wild.

cards.title: Anthropic experimental prompt tool APIs retire August 17
cards.summary: The three `/v1/experimental/*_prompt` endpoints and the legacy Workbench UI are being removed in nine days; any automated prompt-engineering pipelines hitting these endpoints will start returning errors after that date. Migrate now—there is no grace period extension.

cards.title: OpenAI Assistants API shuts down August 26 — migrate to Responses API
cards.summary: All `/v1/assistants`, `/v1/threads`, and `/v1/runs` endpoints go dark on August 26 with no further extensions; the migration maps Assistants→Prompts, Threads→Conversations, Runs→Responses. Azure OpenAI Assistants follows the same cutover date via Microsoft Foundry Agents.

cards.title: Ollama v0.32.6 streaming format now matches OpenAI wire spec exactly — breaking change
cards.summary: The `/v1/chat/completions` streaming layout changed: `role` appears only on the first chunk, `finish_reason` on its own final chunk, and `usage` requires `stream_options.include_usage`. Any client that parsed Ollama's previous non-standard chunk shape will break and needs updating.

cards.title: Node.js patches four HIGH severity issues across 22.x, 24.x, and 26.x
cards.summary: The July 29 security release fixes an HTTP/2 header block that bypasses `maxSessionMemory` (no workaround exists), a `dns.resolveAny()` crash on large responses, a stale SQLite iterator that executes post-reset, and an incomplete TLS hostname-verification fix. Update all active Node lines immediately.

cards.title: Anthropic ships mid-conversation system messages as GA on Claude Fable 5, Mythos 5, and Opus 4.8
cards.summary: System messages can now be inserted at any turn index in the conversation array, not just turn 0, enabling mid-thread persona or instruction switching without resetting context. This directly unblocks multi-agent handoff patterns where a routing agent needs to inject instructions before passing control.

cards.title: CSS `gap` Applies to Flex Containers Even When Items Don't Wrap
cards.summary: The `gap` property on a flex container adds space between items regardless of wrapping. Developers often assume it only matters in grid or multi-line flex layouts, then get burned when a single-row flex row has unexpected spacing that `margin` hacks can't cleanly override.
cards.body: Unlike margins, `gap` is owned by the container and distributes space strictly *between* items — never on the outer edges. This means you cannot accidentally create a leading or trailing gap, which is the exact bug that `* + * { margin-left }` tricks introduce. The catch: `gap` doesn't collapse with sibling margins the way block margins do, so mixing the two in the same axis produces additive spacing that's hard to debug. Profile the layout in DevTools with flex overlays before reaching for margin at all.

cards.title: TypeScript Narrows Discriminated Unions at Assignment, Not at Declaration
cards.summary: TypeScript's control-flow narrowing resets to the full union type after any assignment to a variable, even if the assignment is inside a branch that already proved a narrower type. This causes "type was already narrowed but the error still appears" confusion in production code that mutates locals inside async callbacks.
cards.body: When you assign to a variable that TypeScript has already narrowed, the compiler conservatively widens it back to the declared union because the new value could be anything assignable to that union. This is especially painful across `await` boundaries: the type is narrow before the await, but any code path that could assign to the variable after the await forces the compiler to assume the widest possible type again. The fix is to capture the narrowed value in a `const` before the await — `const` variables cannot be reassigned, so narrowing is permanent for their lifetime. This isn't a TypeScript bug; it's correct behaviour given that `let` variables are mutable.

cards.title: Async Route Handlers Silently Swallow Errors in Express 4
cards.summary: Express 4's router is synchronous internally, so a rejected promise from an async handler never reaches your error middleware—it becomes an unhandledRejection instead. Every async route needs explicit forwarding to next(err), or a wrapper that does it automatically.
cards.body: Express 4 invokes route handlers synchronously and has no mechanism to intercept a rejected promise. When an async handler throws, Node emits an unhandledRejection event and your (err, req, res, next) error middleware is never called—the request hangs or gets no response. A one-liner wrap utility that calls .catch(next) is the minimal fix. Express 5 finally handles this natively, but most production codebases are still on v4.

cards.title: SQLAlchemy Lazy Loading Is Illegal Inside AsyncSession
cards.summary: SQLAlchemy's default relationship strategy issues a new SELECT when you access a relationship attribute. In async mode that implicit IO is synchronous and illegal—it raises MissingGreenlet before any data is returned.
cards.body: The ORM's lazy='select' default works transparently in sync sessions because the attribute access can block. An AsyncSession cannot issue IO outside an awaited call, so touching user.orders raises MissingGreenlet at the attribute access site—not at the await, making the traceback confusing. The fix is declaring your loading strategy at query time with selectinload or joinedload so all required data arrives in one awaited round-trip.
cards.code:
from sqlalchemy.orm import selectinload
from sqlalchemy import select

# Raises MissingGreenlet — .orders triggers implicit IO
async with AsyncSession(engine) as session:
    user = await session.get(User, user_id)
    print(user.orders)  # ← crash here

# Fix: eager-load at query time
async with AsyncSession(engine) as session:
    result = await session.execute(
        select(User).options(selectinload(User.orders)).where(User.id == user_id)
    )
    user = result.scalar_one()
    print(user.orders)  # all data arrived in one await

cards.title: `Optional.orElse` Always Evaluates Its Argument
cards.summary: `orElse(T other)` takes a plain value, not a supplier, so Java evaluates the argument expression before checking whether the Optional is empty. Any method call passed to orElse always executes—even when the value is present.
cards.body: Java evaluates method arguments eagerly before the call is dispatched, so the expression inside orElse() runs unconditionally. This is invisible when the default is a constant, but causes wasted DB lookups, object allocations, or side effects whenever the Optional already holds a value. `orElseGet(Supplier<T>)` wraps the default in a lambda so it only runs on empty. Apply the same reasoning to `Map.getOrDefault`—same eager-evaluation trap.

cards.title: Deferred Calls Inside Loops Stack Until Function Return
cards.summary: `defer` is scoped to the enclosing function, not the current block or loop iteration. A loop that opens files and defers their close holds every file descriptor open simultaneously until the function exits.
cards.body: Go's defer statement pushes a call onto a per-function stack that drains when the function returns—not when the enclosing block ends. In a loop processing hundreds of paths, all file handles, DB connections, or mutex unlocks pile up and are released only at the end of the function, exhausting descriptors or connections long before the loop finishes. Wrapping the loop body in an anonymous function gives each iteration its own function scope, so the defer fires immediately at the end of each closure call.

cards.title: Cache Stampede: Every Request Hits the DB When a Hot Key Expires
cards.summary: When a popular cache key expires, all concurrent requests miss simultaneously and query the database in parallel—multiplying DB load by your request rate for that key. The XFetch algorithm prevents this by probabilistically recomputing the value slightly before expiry, requiring no locks.
cards.body: Expiry is a hard boundary: one moment every request hits cache, the next they all miss. At 500 rps on a hot key, a single expiry event triggers 500 concurrent DB queries for identical data. Mutex-based solutions (one worker recomputes, others wait or return stale) add latency spikes. XFetch recomputes early with a probability that rises as TTL approaches, spreading load across time without coordination. The beta parameter controls aggressiveness; delta tracks how long the last recompute took so faster backends recompute less eagerly.
cards.code:
import math, random, time

def xfetch(cache, key, ttl, beta=1.0):
    value, expiry, delta = cache.get_with_meta(key)
    # Probability of early recompute grows as expiry approaches
    if time.monotonic() - beta * delta * math.log(random.random()) >= expiry:
        t0 = time.monotonic()
        value = db_fetch(key)
        delta = time.monotonic() - t0
        cache.set_with_meta(key, value, ttl=ttl, delta=delta)
    return value

cards.title: Oversizing the Connection Pool Degrades Database Throughput
cards.summary: Adding connections beyond a small multiple of the DB host's CPU cores increases context-switching overhead faster than it adds parallelism, and measured throughput drops. The HikariCP team benchmarks peak throughput at `(core_count × 2) + spindle_count` connections per app instance.
cards.body: A database server is a CPU-bound process: when active connections exceed what the OS can schedule concurrently, threads context-switch, TLB pressure rises, and throughput falls even as the connection count climbs. Most teams set max_connections to 100–500 assuming more is better, then scale out app instances without accounting for the total connection count hitting the DB. A pool of 9 on a 4-core SSD host often outperforms a pool of 100 in benchmarks—and horizontal app scaling must keep (pool_size × instance_count) under the DB's total connection budget.
cards.code:
# HikariCP formula — conceptually valid for any pool driver
# spindle_count = 1 for SSD, actual spindle count for HDD arrays
pool_size = (db_core_count * 2) + spindle_count
# 4-core SSD DB host → pool_size = 9 per app instance
# 5 app replicas → 45 total connections (well under pg default 100)

# application.yml (Spring Boot)
spring:
  datasource:
    hikari:
      maximum-pool-size: 9
      minimum-idle: 9
      connection-timeout: 30000  # ms; fail fast, don't queue forever

cards.title: You're designing a notification system that must deliver at least once to 50M users within 5 minutes of a triggered event. Walk me through your architecture.
cards.summary: Tests whether the candidate can reason about fan-out at scale, choose between push and pull models, and handle partial failure without hand-waving.
cards.body: Start with an event ingress service that writes to a durable log (Kafka). A fan-out worker consumes events and resolves the audience via a pre-materialized subscription index, not a live DB query. Partition delivery workers by user-ID hash so each partition owns a deterministic slice. Use a two-phase approach: enqueue per-user delivery records into a sharded queue, then channel-specific workers (push, email, SMS) drain those queues with idempotent delivery and exponential back-off. At-least-once semantics come from not acknowledging the queue message until downstream confirms. Track delivery state in a lightweight store keyed by (event_id, user_id) so retries are cheap and dedup is possible on the read path. To hit the 5-minute SLA, auto-scale delivery workers on queue depth and pre-warm channel connections.
followUps: How would you handle a channel provider (e.g., APNS) returning rate-limit 429s without violating the 5-minute SLA for other users?
If a single event targets 50M users but a second event targeting 1K VIP users arrives moments later, how do you prevent head-of-line blocking?

cards.title: Explain how backpressure propagates through a Node.js Transform stream pipeline and what happens when you ignore it.
cards.summary: Probes understanding of the streams internal buffering model, highWaterMark, and the real-world consequences of unbounded memory growth.
cards.body: Every Readable and Writable stream has an internal buffer bounded by highWaterMark. When a downstream Writable's buffer fills, its write() returns false, which signals the upstream to stop pushing. In a pipeline created with stream.pipeline(), this signal propagates automatically: the Transform pauses its _read calls, which in turn stops pulling from the source Readable. If you ignore backpressure — say, by calling push() in a loop without checking the return value — the internal buffer grows without limit, heap usage climbs, and the process eventually OOMs or triggers excessive GC pauses that stall the event loop. A common real-world mistake is piping a fast database cursor into a slow HTTP response without respecting drain events. The fix is either to use pipeline() which wires up backpressure and error handling, or to manually listen for 'drain' on the writable side before resuming reads.
followUps: How does objectMode change the meaning of highWaterMark, and why does that matter for memory?
If you need to fan out one Readable to two Writable destinations with different throughput, how do you manage backpressure without blocking the faster consumer?
How would you detect backpressure issues in production without adding stream-level instrumentation to every pipeline?

cards.title: Why can reading offsetHeight between DOM writes cause layout thrashing, and how does the browser's rendering pipeline make this expensive?
cards.summary: Tests knowledge of the browser's layout invalidation model and the real cost of synchronous reflow — not just the buzzword, but the mechanism.
cards.body: The browser batches style and layout calculations and normally performs them once per frame during the rendering pipeline (Style → Layout → Paint → Composite). When JavaScript mutates a layout-affecting property (e.g., setting element.style.width), the layout is marked dirty but not immediately recalculated. However, reading a geometry property like offsetHeight forces the engine to synchronously compute layout right then so it can return a correct value. If you alternate writes and reads in a loop, each read triggers a full or partial layout recalculation — potentially O(n) reflows instead of one. This is layout thrashing. The fix is to batch all reads first (or cache them), then do all writes, which lets the browser coalesce into a single reflow. Libraries like fastdom formalize this read/write scheduling. In frameworks like React this is less common because the virtual DOM batches mutations, but it still appears in refs, imperative animation code, and third-party DOM libraries.
followUps: How does contain: layout CSS property help limit the blast radius of a forced reflow?
In what scenarios can getComputedStyle trigger a style recalculation even without a layout reflow, and why is that distinction important?

cards.title: typeof null and equality
cards.summary: Tests understanding of the typeof null bug, loose vs strict equality between null and undefined.
cards.explanation: typeof null returns "object" due to a legacy spec bug, so the first comparison is true. typeof undefined is "undefined", making the second true. The spec defines null == undefined as true under abstract equality, but null === undefined is false because strict equality requires matching types.

cards.title: Python list comprehension scoping
cards.summary: Tests whether the loop variable in a Python 3 list comprehension leaks into the enclosing scope.
cards.code:
x = 10
result = [x for x in range(3)]
print(x)
print(result)
cards.explanation: In Python 3, list comprehensions have their own implicit scope—the iteration variable x is local to the comprehension and does not overwrite the outer x. This differs from Python 2, where the loop variable leaked into the enclosing scope, which would leave x as 2. The outer x remains 10, and result is [0, 1, 2].

cards.title: Go defer evaluation order
cards.summary: Tests knowledge of Go's defer LIFO execution order and eager argument evaluation.
cards.explanation: Deferred calls in Go execute in LIFO (last-in, first-out) order when the surrounding function returns. Crucially, the arguments to a deferred call are evaluated immediately at the defer statement, not when the deferred function executes. So the values 0, 1, 2 are captured in order, fmt.Print(3) runs first, then the defers unwind as 2, 1, 0—producing 3210.

cards.title: Java string interning and ==
cards.summary: Tests understanding of compile-time constant folding vs runtime string concatenation and reference equality.
cards.explanation: The expression "hel" + "lo" is a compile-time constant, so the compiler folds it to "hello" and interns it in the string pool—making a == b true. However, c + "lo" involves a non-constant variable c, so the JVM creates a new String object at runtime. This means a == d is false because they are different references, while a.equals(d) is true because the content matches.

cards.title: Gemini image-generation models shut down August 17 — eight days to migrate
cards.summary: Imagen 4 and all Gemini 3 Image generation model endpoints stop returning responses on August 17 with no grace period. Any pipeline hitting these endpoints needs a hard cutover now, not a deprecation-warning handler.

cards.title: OpenAI Assistants API goes dark August 26 — threads and file attachments lost
cards.summary: All threads, runs, and attached files become permanently inaccessible after August 26; the migration target is the Responses API, or Foundry Agent Service for Azure customers. There is no read-only grace window, so data extraction must happen before the cutoff.

cards.title: OpenAI Codex removes `--full-auto` flag — replace with `--sandbox workspace-write`
cards.summary: The flag was already deprecated; it is now fully removed, so any CI script or agent runner passing `--full-auto` throws an unrecognised-argument error immediately. Swap in `--sandbox workspace-write` to restore equivalent behaviour.

cards.title: Gemini 3.6 Flash reaches GA; `temperature`, `top_p`, `top_k` deprecated across all Gemini models
cards.summary: The sampling parameter deprecation is the breaking part: callers that pass these fields will hit API errors at the next model version, so remove them proactively regardless of which Gemini model you target. 3.6 Flash itself is cheaper than 3.5 Flash with improved agentic planning.

cards.title: Claude Code self-hosted environments enter public beta for Team and Enterprise
cards.summary: Sessions now run on your own compute with internal network access, custom tooling mounts, and compliance controls — no agent traffic routed through Anthropic infrastructure. Both fixed and on-demand runners are supported, which matters for air-gapped or VPC-locked environments.

cards.title: LLM CLI v0.32 adds streamed reasoning traces, native Responses API, and server-side tools
cards.summary: You can now watch model reasoning stream in real time and call WebSearch or CodeInterpreter as server-side tools without client scaffolding — useful for scripting multi-step workflows. The content-addressed SQLite log store also deduplicates blobs, cutting disk usage on repeated runs.

cards.title: CSS Grid's `auto-fill` vs `auto-fit` Collapse Behaviour
cards.summary: `auto-fill` keeps empty column tracks alive, stretching existing items only when you use `minmax`. `auto-fit` collapses empty tracks to zero, letting filled items grow to fill the row — and the difference only becomes visible when items don't span the full container width.
cards.body: When you write `repeat(auto-fill, minmax(200px, 1fr))`, the browser creates as many 200px-minimum columns as fit, but empty tracks still occupy space — items won't stretch beyond their `1fr` share of the non-empty tracks. Switch to `auto-fit` and those ghost tracks collapse, so a single item in a 3-column grid expands to full width. This trips people up in responsive card grids where the last row has fewer items than expected and they wonder why the cards don't stretch. The distinction is invisible until the number of grid items is fewer than the maximum column count.

cards.title: TypeScript Narrows Union Types Inside Callbacks — But Loses It After an Await
cards.summary: TypeScript's control-flow narrowing does not survive across `await` boundaries because another microtask could theoretically mutate the binding between suspension points, so the compiler resets the type to its declared width after every `await`.
cards.body: If you narrow a variable — say, checking `if (value !== null)` — TypeScript trusts that narrowing for the rest of the synchronous block. But the moment you `await` anything inside that block, the compiler discards the narrowed type on the original variable, even if you know nothing could have changed it. This is because `let` bindings are re-evaluated after each await point; the fix is to capture the narrowed value in a `const` before awaiting. The same issue silently appears with class property checks: narrowing `this.socket` to non-null doesn't survive an await inside the same method.

cards.title: process.nextTick Starves the I/O Queue
cards.summary: process.nextTick callbacks drain their entire queue before Node.js advances to any other event loop phase—including I/O and timers. A recursive nextTick loop will permanently block pending network or file callbacks.
cards.body: The event loop has distinct phases: timers, pending callbacks, poll, check, and close. process.nextTick sits outside all of them in a special queue that must empty completely before the loop moves on. setImmediate runs in the check phase, after I/O, so it yields control between iterations. Swapping a recursive nextTick for setImmediate is the standard fix when you need to defer CPU work without starving the network stack.

cards.title: Unawaited asyncio Tasks Can Be Silently Garbage Collected
cards.summary: asyncio.create_task() schedules a coroutine on the event loop but the returned Task object is only weakly referenced internally. Drop the return value and the GC can cancel the task mid-execution.
cards.body: Unlike directly awaiting a coroutine, create_task lets work run concurrently—but only while a strong reference to the Task exists somewhere. Python 3.12+ emits a warning when a task is destroyed before finishing; earlier versions discard it silently with no traceback. The idiomatic fix is a module-level set: add the task on creation, attach a done callback that discards it, and the reference lives exactly as long as the work does.
cards.code:
import asyncio

_tasks: set[asyncio.Task] = set()

def fire_and_forget(coro):
    task = asyncio.create_task(coro)
    _tasks.add(task)
    task.add_done_callback(_tasks.discard)
    return task

cards.title: @Transactional Self-Calls Bypass the Spring Proxy
cards.summary: Spring's transaction support works through a proxy that wraps your bean at injection time. Calling a @Transactional method from another method on the same class goes through this, not the proxy, so no transaction is ever opened.
cards.body: Spring AOP proxies only intercept calls that arrive from outside the bean—an internal this call reaches the real object directly and skips every piece of advice, including @Cacheable and @Async for the same reason. Private methods can never be intercepted regardless of what annotations they carry. The canonical fix is extracting the transactional method into a separate @Service bean and injecting it, so the call crosses a proxy boundary.

cards.title: Goroutine Closures Capture Loop Variables by Reference
cards.summary: Before Go 1.22, a range loop creates one variable that is mutated each iteration. Goroutines closed over it all see the final value, not the value at launch time.
cards.body: The classic symptom is N goroutines that all process the last element. Passing the value as a function argument creates a per-invocation copy—the pre-1.22 standard fix. Go 1.22 changed range semantics so each iteration binds its own variable, but this only applies when the go directive in go.mod is >= 1.22; older module configurations still have the bug even on a new toolchain.

cards.title: Read Replicas Break Read-Your-Writes Consistency
cards.summary: Async replication means a replica can lag the primary by milliseconds to seconds. A user who writes and immediately reads may hit a replica that hasn't applied their write yet, making their own change appear missing—with no error raised.
cards.body: This failure mode is called read-your-writes (or monotonic reads) and it fails silently—the application gets stale data, not an exception. The cheapest mitigation is routing reads that follow a write back to the primary for the remainder of that request context. Alternatively, track the replication LSN after a write and block replica reads until they confirm they've replayed past that position—Postgres exposes this via pg_wal_lsn_diff.
cards.code:
-- Check live replication lag across all replicas
SELECT
  client_addr,
  state,
  pg_wal_lsn_diff(
    pg_current_wal_lsn(), sent_lsn
  ) AS send_lag_bytes,
  write_lag,
  replay_lag
FROM pg_stat_replication;

cards.title: PgBouncer Transaction Mode Silently Breaks Session-Level Features
cards.summary: In transaction mode, PgBouncer assigns a backend connection per transaction, not per client session. Any feature that assumes a stable session—advisory locks, LISTEN, SET, named prepared statements—fails silently or bleeds state across clients.
cards.body: pg_advisory_lock ties a lock to the backend PID; when PgBouncer reassigns that connection after the transaction ends, the lock releases or is now held under the wrong client's context. A session-level SET made by one client will persist on that backend and be visible to whichever client gets it next. Named prepared statements are stored per backend connection, so a client that prepares on one connection may attempt to execute on another that has never seen it. Session mode is safe but only multiplexes idle connections, sharply reducing the scalability benefit.
cards.code:
# pgbouncer.ini
[pgbouncer]
# transaction mode: advisory locks, LISTEN, SET all unsafe
pool_mode = transaction

# session mode: safe, but one server conn held per client
# pool_mode = session

# This silently misfires in transaction mode:
# SELECT pg_advisory_lock(42);
# -- connection returned to pool here --
# SELECT pg_advisory_unlock(42); -- wrong backend

cards.title: You're designing a notification system that must deliver to 50 million users within 5 minutes of a breaking-news event. Walk me through your architecture.
cards.summary: Tests whether you can reason about fan-out strategies, backpressure, and the trade-offs between push and pull at scale.
cards.body: Start with a topic-based pub/sub layer (e.g., SNS, Kafka) that decouples the editorial publish from delivery. Partition users into segments and fan out to per-channel workers — push notifications, WebSockets, email — each with its own queue and rate-limit contract with the downstream provider. Use consistent hashing to assign user segments to worker pools so you can scale horizontally and reason about per-partition throughput. For the 5-minute SLA, back-of-envelope: 50M / 300s ≈ 167K sends/sec, which means you need to parallel-dispatch across hundreds of workers and pre-compute device tokens in a read-optimized store. Add a dead-letter queue for transient failures and an idempotency key per (user, event) pair so retries don't double-deliver. Monitor p99 delivery latency per channel and auto-scale workers when queue depth crosses a threshold.
followUps: How would you handle a user who is subscribed on three devices without sending duplicate visible notifications?
If your push-notification provider starts returning 429s mid-fan-out, how do you adapt without blowing the SLA?

cards.title: Explain what happens inside the Node.js event loop when a resolved Promise callback and a setTimeout(fn, 0) are both pending. Which fires first, and why?
cards.summary: Tests understanding of the microtask queue vs. the macrotask (timer) phase — a mechanism that affects real-world ordering bugs in server code.
cards.body: When the current execution context completes, the engine drains the microtask queue before the event loop advances to the next phase. Promise .then/.catch/await continuations are microtasks; setTimeout callbacks are macrotasks scheduled in the timers phase. So a resolved Promise callback always fires before a setTimeout(fn, 0) that was registered in the same tick. Internally, libuv's event loop has ordered phases — timers, pending callbacks, poll, check, close — and microtasks are flushed between every phase transition and after every macrotask. This means if a microtask enqueues another microtask, both run before any timer fires, which can starve I/O if you recurse. Node added process.nextTick before microtasks existed; nextTick callbacks also drain before Promises, giving it even higher priority. Understanding this hierarchy is essential for debugging subtle ordering issues in middleware chains and stream pipelines.
followUps: What happens if a process.nextTick callback recursively schedules another nextTick — how does that affect I/O?
How does queueMicrotask differ from process.nextTick, and when would you choose one over the other?
In worker_threads, does each worker get its own event loop and microtask queue?

cards.title: React 18 batches state updates inside event handlers. Describe a concrete scenario where this batching doesn't apply and what you'd do about it.
cards.summary: Tests whether you understand the boundaries of React's automatic batching and the async edge cases that trip up production code.
cards.body: In React 17 and earlier, updates inside native async callbacks (setTimeout, fetch .then, addEventListener outside React) were not batched — each setState triggered a separate render. React 18's createRoot enables automatic batching everywhere, including Promises and timeouts. However, batching still breaks when you opt into synchronous flushing with flushSync: each flushSync(setState) forces an immediate render, which is sometimes needed when you must read the updated DOM before the next update (e.g., measuring an element's height to set a scroll position). Another edge case is updates from external stores (like a Redux middleware callback or a WebSocket message handler using the legacy ReactDOM.render root) — these may bypass batching if the root isn't created with createRoot. The practical fix is to ensure the app uses createRoot and avoid flushSync unless DOM measurement demands it. When you must call flushSync, isolate it and keep the synchronous update minimal to avoid layout thrashing.
followUps: How does React decide when to flush a batch — is it a microtask, a MessageChannel callback, or something else?
If you wrap two setState calls in flushSync, do you get one render or two?

cards.title: Python Mutable Default Arguments
cards.summary: Tests understanding of how mutable default arguments are shared across function calls in Python.
cards.code:
def append(val, lst=[]):
    lst.append(val)
    return lst

print(append(1))
print(append(2))
cards.explanation: Python evaluates default arguments once at function definition time, not at each call. The list object bound to `lst` is shared across all calls that don't supply it. The first call mutates it to [1]; the second call finds [1] already there and appends 2, yielding [1, 2].

cards.title: JavaScript typeof Quirks
cards.summary: Probes knowledge of typeof's counterintuitive results for null, arrays, and NaN.
cards.explanation: typeof null returns "object" due to a legacy bug in the original JS implementation where null's internal type tag was 0, the same as objects. Arrays are objects in JavaScript, so typeof returns "object" — there is no "array" type tag. NaN stands for Not-a-Number but is itself of type "number" per IEEE 754.

cards.title: Go defer and LIFO Order
cards.summary: Tests whether the reader knows deferred calls execute in LIFO order and that arguments are evaluated eagerly.
cards.explanation: Deferred function calls in Go are pushed onto a stack and executed in LIFO order when the surrounding function returns. The argument to fmt.Print is evaluated at the time of the defer statement, not when it executes, so the values 0, 1, 2 are captured. After fmt.Print(3) runs, the defers fire in reverse: 2, 1, 0, producing "3210".

cards.title: Java String Pool and == vs equals
cards.summary: Checks understanding of compile-time string constant folding versus runtime concatenation and reference equality.
cards.explanation: The javac compiler folds the compile-time constant expression "hel" + "lo" into "hello", which is interned in the string pool — so a == b is true. The += operator on c invokes StringBuilder at runtime, producing a new String object not in the pool, so a == c is false. The equals() method compares character content, so a.equals(c) is true.
